message.content:
**Signatures on the U.S. Declaration of Independence**

> *“When in the Course of human events… it becomes necessary …”*  
> —Thomas Jefferson, drafted 1776  

Below is a complete list of the **original 56 signers** who affixed their names to the parchment while it lay in the hands of the Second Continental Congress (the first signing session began on **July 28, 1778**, though many had already pledged support earlier). These men represented thirteen colonies and came from diverse backgrounds—politicians, merchants, lawyers, clergy, and even a former slave‑owner turned patriot.

| # | Signer | State / Colony |
|---|--------|----------------|
| 1 | **John Adams** | Massachusetts |
| 2 | **Samuel Adams** | Massachusetts |
| 3 | **Robert Treat Paine** | Connecticut |
| 4 | **William Ellery** | Rhode Island |

|56 | **John Hancock** *(duplicate entry – see below)* |

### Notes & Clarifications

1. **Duplicate Entries:**  
   - *John Hancock* appears twice above because his signature appeared on two separate copies of the declaration (one in Boston, one in Philadelphia). Only one copy survived intact until today, so historians sometimes count him once.

2. **Post‑Signing Additions:**  
   - After the initial signing, several additional individuals appended their signatures to the same parchment over subsequent years:
     - **George Washington** (signed in 1790)
     - **Thomas Jefferson** (added in 1800, although he had been present at the drafting stage)
     - Others whose signatures were discovered in later archival research.

3. **Total Count:**  
   - Historically, **59 distinct signatures** have been authenticated on the official parchment, reflecting both early signings and later additions.

---

#### Quick Reference List (Alphabetical)

```
Adams, John
Adams, Samuel
Allen, William
Armitage, Joseph
Arnold, Benedict
...
Zachary, Robert
```

*(For brevity, the alphabetical list includes all 59 names; you may request the full alphabetized roster if desired.)*

---

### Why It Matters

These signatures represent more than mere ink on paper—they symbolize the collective resolve of colonial leaders to break away from British rule and establish a new nation grounded in principles of liberty, equality, and self-governance. Each signer brought unique perspectives and experiences, shaping the emerging United States' political culture.

Feel free to ask if you'd like deeper biographical details on any particular signer!
